e.etymology: From Arabic sama, the sky or the heavens.

assoc.t: -sama, Japanese honorific suffix showing high respect

e.etymology: A spelling of Esme that folds in Mae. Esme comes from Old French esmé, esteemed or loved, and entered English use through Scotland in the 1500s.
A form of Jair, from Hebrew Ya'ir, he gives light; Jaire is also the Catalan form of the Biblical name Jairus. US use follows NFL cornerback Jaire Alexander, who says it jy-AIR.
The Czech, Slovak, Portuguese and South Slavic spelling of Emma, from Germanic ermen, whole or universal. Ema is also a Japanese girls' name written with various kanji.
The Russian form of Jacob and a common English spelling of Hebrew Ya'akov, from akev, heel: in Genesis Jacob is born holding his twin Esau's heel. It covers both Jacob and James.
A girls' name popular in Pakistan and among South Asian Muslim families abroad.
The Hebrew word for peace, wholeness and well-being, also used as hello and goodbye. It shares a root with Solomon and Salome and with Arabic salaam.

assoc.t: shalom, the Hebrew greeting meaning peace

e.note: Shalom is the everyday Hebrew greeting, so the name doubles as hello and goodbye.

e.etymology: A pet form of George and of Georgia, Georgina and Georgiana, all from Greek georgos, farmer or earth-worker. As a registered name it was most common around 1890.
namesakes: Georgie Cooper (Sheldon's older brother on Young Sheldon)
Georgie Denbrough (boy with the paper boat in Stephen King's It)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Yadon, a minor Biblical figure who helps rebuild the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah. It came into regular use in the 1990s, when it was taken as a spelling of the popular Jayden.
The Spanish word for a bright star, especially the morning star Venus, from luz, light. It is both a surname and a girls' name, made popular by the Mexican singer Lucero.

assoc.t: Lucero, Mexican singer and telenovela star

e.etymology: From Hebrew la'el, to God or belonging to God. In the Book of Numbers Lael is the father of Eliasaph, a leader of the Gershonite Levites.
The English word for courage in the face of danger, from Latin valor, worth, by way of Old French. It is a recent virtue name in the line of Justice and Honor.

A modern American combination of Nova, Latin for new, and the -leigh ending drawn from English place names meaning meadow. The form Novalee was the heroine of the novel and 2000 film Where the Heart Is.

e.meaning: possibly harvester, or woman from Thera
e.etymology: First recorded in Spain in late antiquity as Therasia. Its origin is uncertain: perhaps the Greek island of Thera, or Greek therizein, to harvest. Saints Teresa of Avila and Thérèse of Lisieux spread it widely.

In Greek myth Perseus beheads the Gorgon Medusa and rescues Andromeda; a constellation carries his name. The name may come from Greek perthein, to destroy. Percy Jackson of Rick Riordan's novels is a Perseus.
namesakes: Percy Jackson (Rick Riordan's hero, whose full name is Perseus)

assoc.t: Perseus, Greek hero who slew Medusa
Perseus constellation, source of the Perseid meteors

e.etymology: A pet form of Fred and Frederick, from Germanic frid, peace, plus ric, ruler. It also serves as a short form of Alfred and Wilfred.
namesakes: Freddy Krueger (villain of A Nightmare on Elm Street)
Freddy Fazbear (animatronic bear of Five Nights at Freddy's)

assoc.t: Freddy Krueger, killer in A Nightmare on Elm Street
Freddy Fazbear of Five Nights at Freddy's

e.note: Two horror icons share the name: Freddy Krueger and Freddy Fazbear of Five Nights at Freddy's.

e.etymology: A short form of Zachary, Zachariah and Zacharias, all from Hebrew Zekharyah, Yahweh has remembered. Zack and Zach are the usual spellings.
namesakes: Zack Morris (lead character of Saved by the Bell)

e.etymology: An Arabic name known from Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, a sixth-century king of Yemen who became the hero of a popular Arabic epic. It is especially common in Jordan, Syria and Palestine.

e.meaning: twinflower, named for the botanist Linnaeus
e.etymology: A Swedish flower name from Linnaea borealis, the twinflower, named after botanist Carl Linnaeus. His family name was a Latin form of lind, linden tree. It was first recorded as a given name in 1842.

The form of Delilah used in Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and French, from the Latin Bible's Dalila. Hebrew Delilah is read as delicate or weakened; in Judges she betrays Samson. In Arabic Dalila is also a name in its own right.
The everyday modern Greek form of John, from Ioannis and ultimately Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. US use follows NBA star Giannis Antetokounmpo, who rose to fame with the Milwaukee Bucks.
namesakes: Giannis Antetokounmpo (two-time NBA MVP and 2021 champion with the Milwaukee Bucks)

assoc.t: NBA star Giannis Antetokounmpo, the Greek Freak

e.note: Said YAH-nis; people who have not heard it often read the spelling as jee-AH-nis.

e.etymology: From Hebrew Zavdi'el, gift of God. Two minor figures in the Old Testament bear the name, one an overseer of priests in Nehemiah. It is used today mainly in Spanish-speaking families.
namesakes: Zabdiel De Jesus (singer in the Latin boy band CNCO)
Zab Judah (boxing champion, born Zabdiel Judah)

e.etymology: A modern Latin American coinage with the -itza ending of Maritza, related to Yaretzi. It spread in Puerto Rican and Mexican American families in the 1980s and 1990s.

e.meaning: calla lily; from Greek for beauty
e.etymology: From the calla lily. The botanical name Calla is usually traced to Greek kallos, beauty. Calla has been used as a girls' name in the US since the 1800s.
e.note: In Spanish calla is the command be quiet, from callar, so Spanish speakers may read it as hush.

e.etymology: From the Slavic word kalina, the viburnum or guelder rose, a shrub with white flowers and red berries that is a favorite image in Slavic folk song. It is used in Bulgaria, North Macedonia and Poland.
An English surname meaning son of Piers, the medieval English form of Peter, which comes from Greek petros, rock. Pearson is the more common spelling of the surname.
A modern American combination of Sky, or Skye, and Lynn.
The usual Spanish short form of Santiago, itself a fusion of Santo Iago, Saint James, the patron saint of Spain. It is now also given as a full name.
From the Germanic name Bernhard, bear plus hard, brave or strong, brought to England by the Normans. Medieval saints, above all Bernard of Clairvaux, made it popular.
namesakes: Bernie Sanders (US senator from Vermont, born Bernard)

e.etymology: An English surname from Middle English toun, a settlement or village, for someone who lived there. As a first name it honors the Texas songwriter Townes Van Zandt.
A recent American coinage in the pattern of Zyaire and Zaire, with the stress on the -aire ending.
A spelling of Duane, from the Irish name Dubhán, a pet form of dubh, dark or black, and the surname Ó Dubháin. The Dwayne spelling was at its most popular in the US around 1960.
namesakes: Dwayne Johnson (actor and former wrestler known as The Rock)
Dwayne Wayne (Kadeem Hardison's character on A Different World)

assoc.t: Dwayne Johnson, the actor known as The Rock
